extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, students of literature, and educated readers interested in poetics and the defence/theory of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance treatise laying out what poesy is, its kinds, purposes, and how to judge or compose it — arguing poetry’s moral, didactic, and aesthetic functions. Useful for evaluating or producing poetry that aims to teach and delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poesy as art of imitation (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poesy, therefore, is an art of imitation; for so Aristotle termeth it in the word μίμησις; that is to say, a representing, counterfeiting, or figuring forth: to speak metaphorically, a speaking picture, with this end, to teach and delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem by how well it imitates (represents or figures forth) its subject matter to both teach and delight; the image-making or 'speaking picture' quality is central to its effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The twofold end: to teach and delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Poesy is an art ... with this end, to teach and delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem must both instruct (convey knowledge, moral insight, or example) and delight (engage the reader’s imagination and emotions). Delight is not mere ornament but necessary because it moves people toward the lesson taught; judge works by their success at combining both effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general kinds of poesy (chief/divine, philosophical, right poets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of this have been three general kinds: the chief ... which they that did imitate the inconceivable excellencies of God; the second kind ... of them that deal with matter philosophical ... the third, indeed right poets, of whom chiefly this question ariseth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify poems according to their scope and subject: divine/psalmic poetry (religious prophecy and praise), philosophical/technical poetry (moral, natural, historical in verse), and properly imaginative poetry (invention that ranges beyond mere reportage). Each kind has different standards and uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as 'maker' creating 'another nature'
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the poet, disdaining to be tied to any such subjection, lifted up with the vigour of his own invention, doth grow, in effect, into another nature; in making things either better than nature bringeth forth, or quite anew ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poets on their inventive faculty: their ability to create exemplary or idealized figures, situations, or worlds that go beyond mere copying of nature. The poet’s power lies in imaginative construction that models excellence or possible moral forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s moral efficacy: moving readers to virtuous action
rubrics_metrics.description: This purifying of wit, this enriching of memory, enabling of judgment, and enlarging of conceit ... the final end is, to lead and draw us to as high a perfection as our degenerate souls ... can be capable of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central measure of poetry’s value is its capacity to convert knowledge and delight into virtuous conduct — to move readers from appreciation to action. Poems should be evaluated for their capacity to 'plant goodness' not merely display knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority to historian and moral philosopher for teaching virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet; and if not a moderator, even the man that ought to carry the title from them both ... therefore compare we the poet with the historian, and with the moral philosopher; and if he go beyond them both, no other human skill can match him ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging didactic power, consider how a poem combines the historian’s concrete example with the moralist’s general precept: poets teach by made examples and persuasive depiction, not only by abstract rules or mere chronicles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse as chosen raiment, not essence of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparelied verse, being but an ornament, and no cause to poetry, since there have been many most excellent poets that never versified, and now swarm many versifiers that need never answer to the name of poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake versification or rhyme for true poetry. Evaluate the substance (invention, teaching, imaginative power) over mere metrical skill; prose may achieve true poetic imitation; conversely, ornamented verse without invention is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and matter: choose poetic form appropriate to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: These be subdivided into sundry more special denominations; the most notable be the heroic, lyric, tragic, comic, satyric, iambic, elegiac, pastoral, and certain others; some of these being termed according to the matter they deal with; some by the sort of verse they like best to write in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poet has selected a form (e.g., heroic, pastoral, tragic) suited to the subject and purpose. Match of form to matter is a criterion of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured, proportioned language suited to subject’s dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Not speaking table-talk fashion, or like men in a dream, words as they changeably fall from the mouth, but piecing each syllable of each word by just proportion, according to the dignity of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess style: diction, cadence, and rhetorical shaping should be proportionate to the subject’s gravity. Precision and crafted language matter; inappropriate colloquialism or slovenliness are defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as first light-giver and preparer of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: They go very near to ungratefulness to seek to deface that which, in the noblest nations and languages that are known, hath been the first light-giver to ignorance, and first nurse, whose milk by little and little enabled them to feed afterwards of tougher knowledges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should value poetry for its cultural and educational role — its capacity to awaken love of knowledge and prepare less cultivated minds for further learning. Evaluate works also by their ability to kindle intellectual appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of poetic devices (dramatic speeches, passionate description) to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Even historiographers ... have been glad to borrow both fashion and, perchance, weight of the poets; so Herodotus entitled the books of his history by the names of the Nine Muses; and both he, and all the rest that followed him, either stole or usurped, of poetry, their passionate describing of passions, the many particularities of battles ... or long orations, put in the mouths of great kings and captains...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept and evaluate rhetorical/poetical devices when they serve to instruct and move: speeches, vivid depictions, and crafted particulars often teach moral and practical lessons more effectively than dry recounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical invention must be 'reined with learned discretion'
rubrics_metrics.description: To imitate, borrow nothing of what is, hath been, or shall be; but range only, reined with learned discretion, into the divine consideration of what may be, and should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment and restraint are part of skill: inventive freedom should be guided by learned judgment and moral purpose, not reckless fantasy. Evaluate whether imagination is disciplined and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true poets from mere 'versifiers' or 'idle tongues'
rubrics_metrics.description: Although, indeed, the senate of poets have chosen verse as their fittest raiment ... yet apparelied verse ... there have been many most excellent poets that never versified, and now swarm many versifiers that need never answer to the name of poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing authors, distinguish substantive poetic skill (making, invention, didactic power) from mere surface ornament or fashionable wordplay. Beware of forms that imitate poetry without its substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s sacred/prophetic aspect (poet as vates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the Romans a poet was called 'vates,' which is as much as a diviner, foreseer, or prophet ... so heavenly a title did that excellent people bestow upon this heart-ravishing knowledge!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that poetry can possess a quasi-prophetic or sacred authority (as in Psalms); evaluate works that aspire to that dignity by their seriousness, moral depth, and capacity to address profound truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge poetry by 'works' and then by 'parts'
rubrics_metrics.description: Now, therefore, it shall not be amiss, first, to weight this latter sort of poetry by his works, and then by his parts; and if in neither of these anatomies he be commendable, I hope we shall receive a more favourable sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should occur at two levels: the whole work (overall effect, moral purpose, imaginative achievement) and the parts (episodes, characters, lines, figures). A poem should be tested both holistically and component-wise.
